title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling & benchmarking playbook
author: Asha Kapoor
body:
Summary:

This playbook consolidates serving runtime documentation for Redwood Inference: runtime architecture, kernel selection and scheduling policies, profiling and benchmarking procedures, release notes for the runtime, known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki pointers. The goal is a single, actionable reference for engineers operating and evolving the high-throughput inference runtime.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: host and dedicated inference runtime components (scheduler, kernel selector, batching and KV cache, network routing, and observability hooks).
- Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, performance engineers, release managers, and on-call responders.

1) Runtime architecture (high level)

Overview:
- Serving runtime components: request ingress (API layer), smart router, scheduler, kernel selector, execution workers (GPU/CPU workers), KV cache layer, result aggregator, telemetry/metrics exporter, and control plane (config + rollouts).
- Design goals: predictable latency (p50/p95/p99 SLOs), high throughput (tokens/sec), graceful degradation (fallback to lower-cost variants), and cost efficiency (batching + caching + quantization profiles).

Key components and responsibilities:
- Smart router: routes requests by policy (latency, cost, region, model variant). Maintains route policy table and fallbacks.
- Scheduler: groups requests into microbatches, schedules kernels, and enforces tenant isolation. Responsible for resource admission/eviction and backpressure.
- Kernel selector: chooses optimized kernels based on model architecture, input sequence length, device topology, and quantization profile.
- Execution workers: run the selected kernels, manage KV cache lifecycle, and report detailed telemetry (latency per stage, GPU utilization, memory tail).
- KV cache: persistent prefix cache that can be shared across compatible model variants; supports TTL and eviction policies.

Architecture constraints and invariants:
- Short-path must avoid global locks. Scheduler uses lock-free queues per-GPU where possible.
- Kernel selection must be deterministic for a given model variant + sequence length bucket to ensure stable perf profiles.
- Memory budgets are enforced per-tenant and per-model; the scheduler refuses additional requests if anticipated OOM risk > 5%.

2) Kernel scheduling and policies

Goals:
- Maximize GPU utilization while keeping p95 latency under SLO.
- Prefer batching for cost efficiency but maintain latency headroom.

Scheduling primitives:
- Work units: request fragments that can be grouped into a microbatch.
- Sequence length buckets: short (<=64), medium (65-256), long (>256). Kernel choice & batch limits vary by bucket.
- Priority classes: realtime (latency SLO strict), best_effort (throughput), internal/maintenance.

Policy examples (default):
1) Realtime requests: max_batch=8 (short), 4 (medium), 1 (long); max_wait=10ms; preemptible=false
2) Best_effort: max_batch=64 (short), 32 (medium); max_wait=50ms; preemptible=true
3) Canary/internal: isolated allocations with min_reservation 0.1 GPU equivalent

Admission control and backpressure rules:
- Admission uses a predictive estimator: if estimated memory + current usage > reserved_budget * 0.95 -> reject with HTTP 429 and hint header X-RI-Retry-After.
- When GPU compute queue depth > 300ms of queued work, scheduler enters backpressure mode and raises max_wait for best_effort classes by 2x.

Affinity and topology awareness:
- Scheduler prefers co-location of kv cache hot shards with worker GPU to avoid cross-node NVMe/GPU PCIe transfers.
- Multi-GPU model sharding uses NCCL/collectives for attention + kv sync; kernel selector adds a topology penalty to models spanning >1 NVLink hop.

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile a regression)

Purpose: give reproducible steps to identify perf regressions and link them to commit, kernel, or config changes.

Preconditions:
- Repro harness under /infra/bench/serving_harness, authenticated service account, and a staging cluster with identical driver/kernel versions to prod.

Tools used:
- perf (host CPU events), nvprof/nvbench (GPU kernel timelines), Nsight Systems (end-to-end trace), custom per-stage tracer (runtime spans), and token-level latency histograms exported to Prometheus.

Step-by-step profiling:
1. Reproduce a representative load using bench harness: ./bench/run_load.py --model <model> --qps <target> --seq_dist short:0.6,medium:0.3,long:0.1 --duration 15m
2. Capture end-to-end traces on a single worker: nsight-sys --trace-file trace.qdrep --target-pid <pid> --duration 5m
3. Capture GPU kernels: nvprof --profile-from-start off --csv -o nvprof.csv --pid <pid>
4. Collect scheduler metrics and microbatch histograms from /metrics endpoint (prometheus scrape).
5. Correlate timelines: map slow tokens to kernel names and scheduler batch sizes. Use script tools/analysis/correlate_trace.py trace.qdrep nvprof.csv metrics.json -> regression_report.md

Heuristics to identify root cause:
- Increased kernel time by >20% across p95 vs baseline -> kernel regression or input distribution change.
- Larger average batch sizes with p99 rise -> batching starvation or memory thrash.
- Spikes in PCIe/host memcpy time -> topology change or data placement regression.
- Higher variance in kv cache hit rate -> cache eviction policy change or model mismatch.

Acceptable baselines and thresholds:
- p50/p95/p99 tokens generation latency targets (example): p50 < 12ms, p95 < 40ms, p99 < 100ms for short sequences on a single-tenant GPU.
- Kernel execution tail: 95th percentile < 85% of per-kernel timeout (configurable per kernel).

4) Benchmarking suite and process

Bench harness components:
- Synthetic driver: generates request mixes with configurable qps, seq length distribution, payload sizes, and prompt templates.
- Replay driver: replays production traces for exact distribution validation (consent required).
- Measurement collector: aggregates per-token latency, batch sizes, GPU SM% and memory tail, KV cache hit/miss, and egress bytes.

Standard benchmark matrix:
- Models: small (7B), medium (13B), large (70B), and quantized variants (int8, int4).
- Devices: A100-40GB, H100-80GB, and T4 for cost-sensitive runs.
- Workloads: interactive (p95 sensitive), batch (throughput), mixed (50/50 chat + summarize).

Benchmark run checklist:
1. Pin drivers and CUDA versions to target release.
2. Warm up for 5 minutes at 30% target QPS.
3. Run three 15-minute iterations for each cell in the matrix.
4. Keep environment variables fixed: RUNTIME_KERNEL_PROFILE=release, KV_CACHE_TTL=120s, SCHEDULER_STRICT=true
5. Collate results into /bench/results/<run_id>. Use tools/bench/aggregate_to_csv.py to create summary CSV and a perf dashboard upload.

Interpreting results:
- Use tokens/sec normalized to device FLOPs to compare across hardware.
- Watch p99 regressions between quantized and FP16 variants when sequence length > 256 (common root cause: attention kernel numeric fallback).

5) Release notes (recent runtime release)

Version: runtime-v5.3.0 (2027-09-15)
Highlights:
- Kernel selector improvements: deterministic kernel binding for medium sequence buckets -> reduced variance in p99 by ~18% in internal benchmarks.
- Scheduler: new preemption window for realtime class reduced tail for mixed workloads by 10-15%.
- Profiling: added NVTX tagging for microbatch boundaries and improved trace correlation scripts.
- Bug fixes: fixed a corner OOM when using int4 quantization with kv cache size > 128MB.

Upgrade notes and compatibility:
- Driver requirement: NVIDIA driver >= 535.86 and CUDA 12.2.
- Rolling upgrade guidance: upgrade control plane first, then workers in a canary pool of 5% traffic for 2 hours, validate p95/p99, then roll remaining workers.

6) Known issues and workarounds

RI-K001: Intermittent p99 spikes for long sequence prompts on H100 when mixed with short seq traffic.
- Symptoms: p99 latency spikes only when mixed workload present.
- Root cause: cross-task KV cache eviction + multi-stream kernel scheduling races.
- Mitigation: set SCHEDULER_STRICT=true on affected pools; as a workaround, isolate long sequence traffic to dedicated pools.

RI-K002: Occasional CUDA driver assertion when loading quantized int4 kernels after warm restart.
- Symptoms: worker crash logs show "cudaErrorIllegalAddress" during kernel init.
- Mitigation: restart affected worker; ensure kernel cache cleared (rm -rf /var/lib/ri/kernel_cache/*) before restart. Patch scheduled in v5.3.1.

RI-K003: KV cache hot shard imbalance after model variant swap.
- Symptoms: hot shard concentrated on a single node causing local OOM.
- Mitigation: run tools/cache/rebalance.py --model <model> to redistribute shards and temporarily increase KV_CACHE_TTL to 300s during migration.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)

High latency incident (p95/p99 breach)
1. Triage: check Grafana dashboard 'runtime/p95-p99' and identify affected pools and models.
2. Run /ops/checklist/latency_triage.sh <pool> to fetch recent traces and kernel breakdown.
3. If kernel regressions indicated, escalate to owning runtime team (tag @serving-runtime).
4. If backlog/backpressure observed, temporarily reduce max_batch for best_effort pools and increase preemption window for realtime pools.
5. If KV cache hit rate degraded, run cache rebalance and consider increasing TTL.
6. Postmortem: create an incident page in confluence under oncall_and_incident_response/postmortems and follow standard postmortem template.

Worker OOM or repeated CUDA errors
1. Isolate worker via control plane: mark node drain=true.
2. Capture syslog and /var/crash, collect nvml logs (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv).
3. Clear kernel cache and restart worker service: systemctl restart ri-worker.
4. If problem reproduces, perform a canary rollback to previous runtime version on the canary pool and open an urgent PR.

Rollout checklist for runtime release
- Pre-merge: run full benchmark matrix and post results to bench dashboard.
- Canary: 5% traffic for 120 minutes, monitor p95/p99, GPU SM and mem tail.
- Progressive: 25% -> 50% -> 100% with 30-60 minute waits depending on risk profile.
- Rollback: automatic if p99 increases by >25% or error rate >0.5% sustained for 10 minutes.

8) Team wiki & onboarding pointers
- Ownership: serving runtime (team page) — owners: @asha_kapoor (tech lead), @miguel_santos (SRE), @lena_zhou (perf).
- Key links: runbook index (/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks), benchmark results dashboard, perf tools repo (git:internal/redwood/serving/perf_tools).
- New engineer checklist: read this playbook, run bench harness in staging, complete profiling lab (guide under /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-lab).

Appendix: example scheduler config (YAML)

# scheduler.yml
# NOTE: all values shown are examples, control plane UI is authoritative
scheduler:
  default_policies:
    realtime:
      max_batch_short: 8
      max_batch_medium: 4
      max_wait_ms: 10
      preemptible: false
    best_effort:
      max_batch_short: 64
      max_wait_ms: 50
      preemptible: true
  admission:
    memory_headroom_pct: 5
    backpressure_queue_ms: 300

Contact and escalation:
- For immediate pager: @serving-runtime on PagerDuty (primary: Miguel Santos).
- For kernel selection or perf regressions: Asha Kapoor (lead).

This document will be kept up to date alongside runtime releases and benchmarking results. If you find missing steps or inconsistent guidance, file a PR to the confluence page or raise directly in the serving-runtime channel.
